items.questionAndWhy: Can changing what older adults emphasize during training improve selective attention?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers manipulated instructional emphasis during an attention-training task with older adults.
items.whatTheyFound: Training effects depended on what participants were asked to prioritize, with selective benefits rather than broad cognitive improvement.
items.whatItMeans: Instructional framing can change what is learned; transfer should be measured separately from trained-task gains.
items.streamTitle: Changing training emphasis altered selective-attention gains in older adults
items.streamSummary: An experiment with older adults found that what participants were instructed to emphasize during attention training changed the pattern of improvement. Benefits were selective rather than evidence of a general cognitive boost. The result is relevant to training design because task instructions can become part of the intervention; transfer beyond the practiced task still needs separate evidence.

items.questionAndWhy: Does perceived ethnicity affect investor support after a venture founder has experienced failure?
items.whatTheyDid: A conjoint experiment varied founder and venture attributes, including Latinx identity and prior failure.
items.whatTheyFound: Latinx founders faced different post-failure funding evaluations under some conditions, indicating that failure signals can interact with identity.
items.whatItMeans: Decision biases can be conditional rather than constant; models should represent how identity and prior outcomes interact.
items.streamTitle: Founder identity changed how prior failure affected funding judgments
items.streamSummary: A conjoint experiment examined how investors evaluate founders after prior venture failure. Results indicated that Latinx identity interacted with failure-related judgments under some conditions rather than producing one constant penalty. The study concerns stated investment choices in an experimental design, not observed capital flows, but it shows why bias can emerge through interactions between identity and performance history.

items.questionAndWhy: How tightly are speech gestures coupled to whole-body postural control?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers measured co-speech gesture and postural sway during speaking tasks.
items.whatTheyFound: Gesture production covaried with postural dynamics, suggesting speech-related movement is embedded in a broader motor system.
items.whatItMeans: Behavioral signals should not be interpreted in isolation when several bodily processes are mechanically or temporally coupled.
items.streamTitle: Co-speech gestures were coupled with whole-body postural dynamics
items.streamSummary: A laboratory study measured gestures and postural sway during speech and found coordinated changes between the two. The result suggests that visible communicative movement is embedded in a wider motor system rather than being an isolated channel. It does not establish a psychological meaning for any one posture signal, but it cautions against treating body-language features as independent indicators.

items.questionAndWhy: Can vectorized reinforcement-learning simulation accelerate control learning for microrobots?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers built a highly parallel simulation environment and trained reinforcement-learning controllers for microrobotic tasks.
items.whatTheyFound: Vectorization accelerated training and produced effective policies in simulation, with transfer limitations remaining for physical systems.
items.whatItMeans: Fast simulation expands experimentation, but sim-to-real validity remains the central operational question.
items.streamTitle: Vectorized simulation accelerated reinforcement learning for microrobot control
items.streamSummary: A machine-learning study used vectorized simulation to train microrobot control policies at much higher throughput. The reported policies performed well in the simulated tasks, showing how parallel environments can reduce training cost. The evidence does not eliminate sim-to-real uncertainty: physical noise, sensing, and actuation can change performance when policies leave the simulator.

items.questionAndWhy: Can temporal network motifs improve identification of important nodes in dynamic systems?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers modeled recurring temporal interaction motifs and compared node-ranking methods.
items.whatTheyFound: Motif-aware ranking captured dynamic importance that static network measures missed in the tested datasets.
items.whatItMeans: For influence or infrastructure networks, temporal ordering can change which nodes appear important; static centrality is not always enough.
items.streamTitle: Temporal motifs changed which nodes appeared important in dynamic networks
items.streamSummary: A Scientific Reports study incorporated recurring temporal motifs into node ranking and found that dynamic interaction patterns can identify importance differently from static network measures. The method is useful when sequence and timing matter, but high rank still does not establish causal leverage, feasibility, or intervention value. Those require separate evidence.

items.questionAndWhy: Can benchmark design test whether agents reason through evolving causal pathways rather than memorize static answers?
items.whatTheyDid: EvoPathBench introduced tasks built around changing multi-step pathways and evaluated agent performance.
items.whatTheyFound: The benchmark exposed degradation as pathways evolved and required agents to update intermediate reasoning rather than rely on fixed retrieval.
items.whatItMeans: Dynamic benchmarks are useful for testing adaptation, but benchmark success still needs external task validation.
items.streamTitle: EvoPathBench tested whether agents can update reasoning as pathways change
items.streamSummary: EvoPathBench is a preprint benchmark for agent reasoning over evolving multi-step pathways. It is designed to expose systems that rely on static retrieval or memorized patterns when intermediate relationships change. Reported results show meaningful performance variation across agents. The benchmark is useful for adaptation testing, but success on synthetic tasks does not itself establish reliable reasoning in real operational systems.

items.questionAndWhy: What happens when wartime strikes target telecommunications and data infrastructure rather than only energy or military assets?
items.whatTheyDid: Reuters documented Russian strikes affecting Kyivstar facilities and Ukrainian data centers, alongside reported service disruptions.
items.whatTheyFound: The attacks damaged communications infrastructure and disrupted services for some users; attribution for specific effects came from operators and officials.
items.whatItMeans: Digital resilience should be measured through service continuity, failover, repair time, and user impact rather than facility damage alone.
items.streamTitle: Russian strikes expanded to Ukrainian telecom and data infrastructure
items.streamSummary: Reuters reported Russian attacks on Ukrainian telecommunications and data infrastructure, including Kyivstar facilities and data centers. Operators and officials described service disruptions affecting communications. The attacks show that digital infrastructure is part of wartime resilience, but physical damage and mission impact are not the same outcome. Recovery time, redundancy, and continuity should be tracked separately.

items.questionAndWhy: How does NATO's top commander interpret sabotage, cyberattacks, and drone incidents as a coercive campaign?
items.whatTheyDid: Reuters reported Gen. Alexus Grynkewich's testimony urging attribution of Russian hybrid actions and describing an objective of weakening allied support for Ukraine.
items.whatTheyFound: The statement provides an official strategic assessment and deterrence argument, not independent proof of every incident's attribution or effect.
items.whatItMeans: Observed incidents, attribution, assessed intent, and measured political effect should remain separate analytical layers.
items.streamTitle: NATO's top commander said hybrid attacks aim to break allied will, while urging public attribution
items.streamSummary: NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Alexus Grynkewich urged governments to attribute sabotage, cyberattacks, and drone activity that he said were intended to weaken support for Ukraine. The statement is an important strategic assessment, not proof that every cited incident was Russian-directed or that the campaign has changed allied behavior. It illustrates the need to separate event, attribution, intent, and effect.

items.questionAndWhy: Can FRAM represent the parallel, variable, sociotechnical work involved in surgical scheduling better than sequential process maps?
items.whatTheyDid: Rashid and colleagues used stakeholder interviews, observation, FRAM modeling, and FRAMalyse to represent 98 interconnected functions across the surgical scheduling pathway.
items.whatTheyFound: The model identified candidate high-variability and high-coupling functions, including surgical-team allocation and central patient management. These are modeled bottlenecks requiring further validation, not measured causal effects.
items.whatItMeans: FRAM is useful for making work-as-done, variability, and coordination explicit. Candidate leverage points should be validated with operational data before intervention.
items.streamTitle: A quantitative FRAM model mapped 98 functions in surgical scheduling and surfaced candidate bottlenecks
items.streamSummary: Researchers applied FRAM and FRAMalyse to a hospital surgical-scheduling process, using interviews and observations to model 98 interconnected functions. The analysis highlighted high-variability and high-coupling activities that could become bottlenecks. The model is a structured representation of sociotechnical work, not proof that changing the highest-ranked function will improve scheduling. Operational validation is the next step.
items.attribution: Rashid et al. — International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery

items.questionAndWhy: What predicts professional football coaches' adoption of AI chatbots, and is age itself the main barrier?
items.whatTheyDid: Ghorbel and colleagues surveyed 213 professional coaches and analyzed a digital-literacy index, adoption, perceived barriers, and performance outcomes using mediation, ROC, ANOVA, and cluster analyses.
items.whatTheyFound: Digital literacy strongly separated adopters from non-adopters and statistically mediated several age- and experience-related relationships. The study is cross-sectional, so the mediation does not establish causal transmission.
items.whatItMeans: Apparent demographic barriers to technology adoption may be partly skill or access differences. Training interventions should test whether raising literacy actually changes use and performance.
items.streamTitle: Digital literacy was strongly associated with AI-chatbot adoption among football coaches
items.streamSummary: An international survey of 213 professional football coaches found that digital literacy was strongly associated with AI-chatbot adoption and statistically accounted for several age- and experience-related differences. The study identified a useful competency threshold in its sample, but the cross-sectional mediation cannot prove that improving digital literacy will cause adoption. A training intervention would be the stronger next test.
